Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: MC-EvoBench is a controlled Minecraft benchmark designed to evaluate and audit the transferability and durability of embodied capabilities in self-improving agents.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: EndoRSI: Physical-Evidence-Driven Recursive Improvement of Endoscopic Robot Policies
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Chi Kit Ng, Yidong Zhang, Tianchun Wu, Siu Hing Lui, Hanlin Zhao
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: EndoRSI is a self-improving robotic system that refines endoscopic policies through iterative physical experimentation and human oversight, significantly enhancing insertion success rates.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot policy research.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Dijia Zhan, Zhuo Li, Xuemiao Xu, Sun Zheng, Jinyi Li
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: The paper presents Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), enhancing autoregressive robot policies by enabling tokens to iteratively refine action reconstructions, improving performance across various tasks.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: Watch, Recall, Act: Always-On Robots in Concurrent Embodied Streams
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Ding Yi, Peiwen Sun, Chenchu Rong, Jianan Wang, Xili Dai
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: The paper introduces ARMS, an always-on robot capable of concurrent actions by integrating live perception and self-history, achieving superior performance in complex, dynamic environments.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: An always-on robot faces an endless stream that never resets: instructions arrive and lapse, the scene changes, and its own past actions reshape what it must reason about. Today's action models are built for the opposite: a fixed instruction, no mid-task intervention, single-step reasoning. In an open-ended world a robot must watch a live stream for far-future cues, recall its own far-past actions, and act on them under dual-arm concurrency. We present ARMS (Always-on Robot in Multi-modal Streams), a deliberately simple streaming policy: a single pretrained $π$0.5 backbone augmented by three lightweight modules that turn live perception, embodied states, and the robot's own past actions into context the backbone reads before it acts. The modules update this context asynchronously, so watching and recalling never block acting and the two arms act at once. Rather than inventing new mechanisms, ARMS integrates these learned context providers with an agent-causal self-history that logs which arm did what, and when. To supervise them without extra annotation, we build ARMS Dataset, whose staged construction script itself labels every module from real dual-arm teleoperation. Trained on it, ARMS reaches 45% on the combined task against 28% for the strongest of our four main baselines, and ablations confirm the memory module, the embodied-state head, and asynchronous concurrency are each necessary.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: TaskAnchor: Grounding Task State in Reactive VLAs for Long-Horizon Manipulation
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Hengyan Liu, Wenlve Zhou, Bo Yue, Yongyi Su, Ruixiang Wang
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: TaskAnchor enhances long-horizon manipulation in reactive VLAs by grounding task state through contextual input adaptation, significantly improving success rates without altering the backbone architecture.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Reactive vision-language-action (VLA) policies suffer from task-state aliasing in long-horizon manipulation, where identical multimodal inputs call for distinct, context-dependent actions. Given that pretrained VLAs already possess rich control primitives to express diverse behaviors, we hypothesize that the execution bottleneck lies not in policy capacity, but in input ambiguity. In this paper, we propose TaskAnchor, a lightweight adapter that grounds task state by injecting execution context into the VLA's native input space. During post-training, TaskAnchor learns to represent the semantic execution stage as a milestone-supervised coordinate prepended to the language instruction, while incorporating fine-grained historical evidence via a residual update to the current visual tokens. This formulation avoids generating complex subtask instructions and leaves the backbone architecture unchanged. Across long-horizon benchmarks, TaskAnchor delivers substantial gains, achieving approximately 6 times the average success rate of the pi0.5 and X-VLA baselines on RMBench and more than doubling the task success rate of pi0.5 on RoboMemArena. Real-robot experiments further validate reliable multi-stage execution, with the same policy adapting its subsequent behaviors using earlier human interactions as in-context cues. Our project website is available at https://taskanchor.netlify.app/.

OpenDriveLab.title: PartiGen: Part-Aware Representations for Language-Conditioned Humanoid Motion Generation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Chuxuan Huang, Zhanxiang Cao, Tianyue Zhan, Haoyang Li, Yang Zhang
OpenDriveLab.summary: PartiGen is a part-aware framework that generates humanoid motion from language by integrating anatomical structure and improving kinematic consistency, achieving significant performance enhancements in simulation and real execution.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Translating language into humanoid motion requires coordinating body parts, determining motion duration, and producing references suitable for robot execution. We introduce PartiGen, a part-aware latent diffusion framework that incorporates anatomical structure into a shared whole-body motion representation. Part-specific attention processes anatomically masked frame features, and its outputs are fused to combine local limb information with whole-body context. Conditioned on text and motion history, the model generates motion primitives autoregressively. Forward-kinematics supervision encourages kinematic consistency, while a learned end-of-sequence predictor selects a frame-level endpoint after generation. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, PartiGen achieves a segment-level FID of 3.165, a 16.8% reduction over TextOp, and improves R@1 by 1.4 percentage points. In the duration study with 16-frame primitives, endpoint prediction reduces mean absolute duration error from 12.471 to 3.080 frames compared with a fixed-length cutoff. We further evaluate robot execution using a pretrained, frozen GRIT tracker: 409 of 500 generated references (81.8%) pass the posture-based stability screen in MuJoCo. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 attempted motions are judged successful on the real G1.

OpenDriveLab.title: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Jie Huang, Yanan Chen, Ruixun Liu, Kaichen He, Xinyi He
OpenDriveLab.summary: EmbodiedCLBench is a novel benchmark for assessing continual learning in self-evolving agents within embodied environments, revealing limitations and insights into skill transfer and task complexity.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.

OpenDriveLab.title: MIRAGE: Metric Inference and Reliability-Aware Gaussian Estimation from Feed-Forward Vision
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Xinzhe Wang, Changjian Jiang, Kaiwen Song, Xudong Li, Kerui Ren
OpenDriveLab.summary: MIRAGE integrates feed-forward visual geometry with LiDAR-IMU data for accurate metric pose estimation and high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction, outperforming existing vision-only methods.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Feed-forward 3D priors enable high-quality reconstruction from image streams but often lack reliable metric scale and suffer from long-term trajectory drift. In contrast, LiDAR--inertial estimation provides metrically accurate motion but lacks the image-space consistency needed for high-fidelity reconstruction. We propose $MIRAGE$, which anchors feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR--IMU metric motion and regulates online pose corrections according to correspondence support and cross-modal agreement, jointly enabling accurate metric pose estimation and high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction. Experiments on Oxford Spires, M2DGR and INS show that MIRAGE achieves accurate metric trajectory estimation, outperforming COLMAP, a widely used but computationally expensive reference for vision-only benchmarks. Motivated by the scarcity of long-horizon monocular benchmarks for large-scale indoor reconstruction, we further build a multimodal data-collection platform and use MIRAGE to establish accurate 6-DoF reference trajectories for a new vision-only benchmark. We benchmark recent monocular large-scale reconstruction methods on this dataset, providing a systematic evaluation of their performance in long-horizon indoor scenes.

OpenDriveLab.title: MagCilia: A Compact Magnetociliary Tactile Sensor with 3D Force Sensing for Robotic Contact Perception and Grasping Feedback
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yu Feng, Hao Wu, Haotian Guo, Haoming Liu, William Su
OpenDriveLab.summary: The MagCilia sensor integrates flexible magnetic-cilia structures and Hall sensors for precise 3D force sensing, enhancing robotic grasping and surface recognition capabilities.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Robotic grasping and surface exploration benefit from simultaneous measurement of normal and tangential forces and from surface information obtained through contact. Here, we present a compact magnetociliary tactile sensor (MagCilia) that combines a flexible magnetic-cilia structure with a Hall sensor for 3D force sensing. Quasi-static finite element analysis is used to investigate structural deformation and magnetic responses under multidirectional loading. To reconstruct forces from the coupled magnetic channels, we propose causal history fusion regression (CHFR), which combines current magnetic-field measurements with their recent changes. Five-fold cross-validation grouped by calibration record yields root-mean-square errors of 0.40, 0.57, and 0.69 N for Fx, Fy, and Fz, respectively, with corresponding coefficients of determination of 0.93, 0.90, and 0.92. Robotic experiments demonstrate tangential-force-guided gripper adjustment and multi-axis load monitoring under external perturbations. Frequency-domain features of the reconstructed forces distinguish six surface categories with 99.39% accuracy in three-fold cross-validation grouped by acquisition session. An online robotic demonstration additionally identifies all six tested surfaces. These results demonstrate 3D force reconstruction, grasping feedback, and surface recognition using a single compact tactile unit.

OpenDriveLab.title: Spatial Memory Intelligence: Endowing World Models with Understanding-Driven Long-Term Memory
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Ying Yang, Guiyu Zhang, Lianghua Huang, Chang Nie, Chenyang Si
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper introduces Spatial Memory Intelligence (SMI), a framework enhancing long-video world models with systematic spatial-memory management through four coordinated operations, improving memory efficiency and generation quality.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Long-video generation and world models have shown strong potential for interactive entertainment and embodied simulation by predicting future observations conditioned on user actions and historical memory. However, as memory sequences grow longer and their structures become increasingly complex, managing long-range spatial context becomes increasingly challenging, calling for a more intelligent and systematic memory-management strategy. Building on the advancing spatial reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and the broader vision of unified models, we propose Spatial Memory Intelligence (SMI), the first framework to systematically employ an understanding model for spatial-memory management in long-video world models. SMI introduces four coordinated atomic operations: spatial clustering, within-cluster sparsification, action-aware retrieval, and reliability-aware filtering. Extensive experiments across multiple baselines, benchmarks, and world-model backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of SMI, achieving comprehensive improvements in memory sparsity, generation stability, and spatial consistency.

OpenDriveLab.title: Object Concepts Emerge from Motion
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Boshi Li, Xiaohui Wang, Xiaoyang Wu, Zhichao Li, Ya Yang
OpenDriveLab.summary: This paper introduces a motion-based framework for learning object-centric visual representations from videos, achieving superior performance in various tasks without requiring human annotations.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Object-centric visual representations are important for physical-world perception, but existing visual pretraining methods often capture semantic categories without preserving the identity and coherence of individual instances. We present a biologically inspired framework that learns object-centric representations for single images from raw videos. Our approach uses motion boundaries as a source of object-level grouping: off-the-shelf optical flow and clustering produce pseudo-instance masks, which supervise a single-image encoder with pixel-level pairwise metric learning. The framework requires neither human annotations nor camera calibration. We first obtain 195 million pseudo-labeled frames from 7,163 hours of driving and web videos, then expand the supervision to 421 million frames with Motion-Verified Self-Training, which combines model proposals with motion evidence. We train encoders up to Swin-H and distill the learned representations into a family of Swin backbones. Across monocular depth estimation, 3D object detection, 3D occupancy prediction, and end-to-end planning, the resulting models achieve competitive or superior performance relative to supervised and self-supervised pretraining baselines, with particularly strong transfer on geometry- and instance-sensitive tasks. These results show that motion-derived supervision can teach static image encoders to represent visual instances, providing a complementary direction for scalable visual pretraining.

OpenDriveLab.title: Latent Reward Steering: An Adaptive Inference-Time Framework that Implicitly Promotes Cognitive Behaviors in Reasoning LLMs
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Jiakang Li, Guanyu Zhu, Can Jin, Chenxi Huang, Dexu Yu
OpenDriveLab.summary: Latent Reward Steering (LRS) enhances reasoning in LLMs by adaptively optimizing latent states based on reward signals, improving cognitive behavior deployment during inference.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Strong reasoning depends not only on model knowledge but also on how effectively cognitive behaviors are deployed during generation. Existing methods often rely on explicit behavior-level control, making them insufficiently adaptive when failures and required corrections vary across reasoning states, tasks, and models. To this end, we propose Latent Reward Steering (LRS), an adaptive inference-time framework that promotes cognitive behaviors by optimizing the sparse-autoencoder (SAE) latent states that implicitly carry them. Rather than relying on predefined cognitive behaviors or steering directions derived from them, LRS trains a latent reward model on reasoning traces by final answer correctness to estimate the quality of intermediate latent states. During inference, reward gradients provide state-specific correction directions for fragile latent states, while a reward and confidence gate restricts intervention to states the reward signal flags as fragile. Experiments on multiple reasoning LLM backbones and benchmarks show that \ours consistently improves performance over various baselines, and post-hoc analyses further indicate that \ours implicitly promotes good cognitive behaviors that fix the original reasoning errors. Code is available at: https://github.com/jiakanglee/Latent-Reward-Steering.

OpenDriveLab.title: SAP-CoPE: Social-Aware Planning using Cooperative Pose Estimation with Infrastructure Sensor Nodes
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Minghao Ning, Yufeng Yang, Shucheng Huang, Jiaming Zhong, Keqi Shu
OpenDriveLab.summary: SAP-CoPE is an indoor navigation framework that combines cooperative sensing, human pose estimation, and social-aware motion planning to enhance robot interactions in human-populated environments.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Autonomous mobile robots must operate smoothly in human-populated indoor environments, where onboard-only sensing suffers from limited perception range and occlusions, and socially compliant motion planning must account for human psychological comfort zones. These factors complicate accurate recognition of human intentions and the generation of comfortable, social-aware trajectories. To address these challenges, we propose SAP-CoPE, an indoor navigation framework that integrates cooperative infrastructure sensing, human pose estimation, and a social-aware MPC planner. In the perception module, an uncertainty-aware optimization problem is formulated to estimate 3D human poses from camera observations, with optional incorporation of sparse LiDAR point-cloud measurements, while considering human joint coherence. In the planning module, the estimated human pose and orientation are used to construct a personal-space (PS) field within an MPC framework, enabling the robot to account for both physical safety and psychological comfort. Extensive real-world evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in generating social-aware trajectories for autonomous systems.

OpenDriveLab.title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yuhong Liu, Shenxi Wu, Junyi Chi, Beichen Zhang, Xuanlang Dai
OpenDriveLab.summary: SpatialASM enhances Large Vision-Language Models by integrating Active Spatial Mentalization through training-time spatial simulation, improving their spatial reasoning capabilities across multiple benchmarks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.

OpenDriveLab.title: SimVTA: Simulation-Grounded Video-Trajectory Alignment for Driving World Action Models
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Changhui Jing, Haochen Tian, Hongchen Li, Tianyu Li, Caojun Wang
OpenDriveLab.summary: SimVTA enhances driving world action models by integrating simulation-grounded video supervision for trajectory optimization, significantly improving planning performance in real-world scenarios.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Driving world action models (WAMs) learn from paired trajectories and future observations. Post-training with reinforcement learning allows the policy to explore alternative trajectories and improve planning using driving rewards. However, driving logs contain future videos only for the recorded trajectories, leaving these alternatives without corresponding visual supervision. Thus, we introduce SimVTA, a simulation-grounded post-training framework that combines trajectory optimization with video supervision. First, we sample candidate trajectories for each observation and use a real-world simulator (e.g., World Engine) to render future videos for high-reward candidates in real-world scenes reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). This provides trajectory-matched supervision independent of the model's own predictions. Under a limited rendering budget, we prioritize video supervision for higher-error futures among these rendered candidates. Finally, we optimize trajectory planning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and use a flow-matching loss on the matched videos to update shared representations. At inference time, the model predicts trajectories directly, without simulator calls. On NAVSIM v1, applying SimVTA to a WAM initialization improves PDMS from 86.2 to 91.3 (+5.1). It achieves 88.2 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and an average HD-Score of 38.8 in closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM. Ablations show that updating shared representations with video supervision improves planning, while prioritizing higher-error futures among high-reward trajectories further improves performance.

OpenDriveLab.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Jingjing Wei, Hao Zhao, Xinke Li, Linxi Yu, Xiaosong Gao
OpenDriveLab.summary: The MathVis benchmark evaluates LLMs' diagram-assisted reasoning in math problem visualization, revealing limitations in their ability to produce clear, visually coherent outputs.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.

OpenDriveLab.title: KineWorld: Action-Induced Transport Fields for Embodied World Modeling
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Ziying Song, Yuchen Liu, Zhuoran Xu, Ziyang Liu, Jian Jin
OpenDriveLab.summary: KineWorld introduces a transport-aware framework for embodied world modeling, enhancing action prediction by aligning visual generation with critical spatial changes in robot interactions.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Embodied world models predict the visual consequences of candidate actions before execution. However, existing action-conditioned world models often adopt uniformly weighted visual generation objectives that can be misaligned with embodied prediction needs. Even with explicit motion conditioning, these objectives can underemphasize spatially sparse changes that are critical to interaction. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs renderer-derived, camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates their motion support on the video-latent grid and reweights future-RGB flow matching through a normalized mixture of uniform and transport-focused distributions. We train KineWorld using ALOHA-AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0. KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 in single-view evaluation and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in multi-view evaluation. These results support a shift from appearance fitting toward action-consequence modeling for embodied decision-making.

OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Hengyan Liu, Wenlve Zhou, Bo Yue, Yongyi Su, Ruixiang Wang
OpenDriveLab.summary: TaskAnchor enhances long-horizon manipulation in reactive VLAs by grounding task state through contextual input adaptation, significantly improving success rates without altering the backbone architecture.

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: PartiGen: Part-Aware Representations for Language-Conditioned Humanoid Motion Generation
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Chuxuan Huang, Zhanxiang Cao, Tianyue Zhan, Haoyang Li, Yang Zhang
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: PartiGen is a part-aware framework that generates humanoid motion from language by integrating anatomical structure and improving kinematic consistency, achieving significant performance enhancements in simulation and real execution.

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: MIRAGE: Metric Inference and Reliability-Aware Gaussian Estimation from Feed-Forward Vision
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Xinzhe Wang, Changjian Jiang, Kaiwen Song, Xudong Li, Kerui Ren

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: MagCilia: A Compact Magnetociliary Tactile Sensor with 3D Force Sensing for Robotic Contact Perception and Grasping Feedback
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Yu Feng, Hao Wu, Haotian Guo, Haoming Liu, William Su
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: The MagCilia sensor integrates flexible magnetic-cilia structures and Hall sensors for precise 3D force sensing, enhancing robotic grasping and surface recognition capabilities.

Frequency-domain features of the reconstructed forces distinguish six surface categories with 99.39% accuracy in three-fold cross-validation grouped by acquisition session. An online robotic demonstration additionally identifies all six tested surfaces. These results demonstrate 3D force reconstruction, grasping feedback, and surface recognition using a single compact tactile unit.

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: Spatial Memory Intelligence: Endowing World Models with Understanding-Driven Long-Term Memory
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Ying Yang, Guiyu Zhang, Lianghua Huang, Chang Nie, Chenyang Si
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: The paper introduces Spatial Memory Intelligence (SMI), a framework enhancing long-video world models with systematic spatial-memory management through four coordinated operations, improving memory efficiency and generation quality.
机器人与自动化研究中心.debug_abstract: Long-video generation and world models have shown strong potential for interactive entertainment and embodied simulation by predicting future observations conditioned on user actions and historical memory. However, as memory sequences grow longer and their structures become increasingly complex, managing long-range spatial context becomes increasingly challenging, calling for a more intelligent and systematic memory-management strategy. Extensive experiments across multiple baselines, benchmarks, and world-model backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of SMI, achieving comprehensive improvements in memory sparsity, generation stability, and spatial consistency.

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: Latent Reward Steering: An Adaptive Inference-Time Framework that Implicitly Promotes Cognitive Behaviors in Reasoning LLMs
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Jiakang Li, Guanyu Zhu, Can Jin, Chenxi Huang, Dexu Yu
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: Latent Reward Steering (LRS) enhances reasoning in LLMs by adaptively optimizing latent states based on reward signals, improving cognitive behavior deployment during inference.
机器人与自动化研究中心.debug_abstract: Strong reasoning depends not only on model knowledge but also on how effectively cognitive behaviors are deployed during generation. Existing methods often rely on explicit behavior-level control, making them insufficiently adaptive when failures and required corrections vary across reasoning states, tasks, and models. To this end, we propose Latent Reward Steering (LRS), an adaptive inference-time framework that promotes cognitive behaviors by optimizing the sparse-autoencoder (SAE) latent states that implicitly carry them. Rather than relying on predefined cognitive behaviors or steering directions derived from them, LRS trains a latent reward model on reasoning traces by final answer correctness to estimate the quality of intermediate latent states. During inference, reward gradients provide state-specific correction directions for fragile latent states, while a reward and confidence gate restricts intervention to states the reward signal flags as fragile. Experiments on multiple reasoning LLM backbones and benchmarks show that \ours consistently improves performance over various baselines, and post-hoc analyses further indicate that \ours implicitly promotes good cognitive behaviors that fix the original reasoning errors. Code is available at: https://github.com/jiakanglee/Latent-Reward-Steering.

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Yuhong Liu, Shenxi Wu, Junyi Chi, Beichen Zhang, Xuanlang Dai
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: SpatialASM enhances Large Vision-Language Models by integrating Active Spatial Mentalization through training-time spatial simulation, improving their spatial reasoning capabilities across multiple benchmarks.
机器人与自动化研究中心.debug_abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: MC-EvoBench is a controlled Minecraft benchmark designed to evaluate and audit the transferability and durability of embodied capabilities in self-improving agents.
机器人与自动化研究中心.debug_abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: EndoRSI: Physical-Evidence-Driven Recursive Improvement of Endoscopic Robot Policies
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Chi Kit Ng, Yidong Zhang, Tianchun Wu, Siu Hing Lui, Hanlin Zhao
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: EndoRSI is a self-improving robotic system that refines endoscopic policies through iterative physical experimentation and human oversight, significantly enhancing insertion success rates.
机器人与自动化研究中心.debug_abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot policy research.

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Dijia Zhan, Zhuo Li, Xuemiao Xu, Sun Zheng, Jinyi Li
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: The paper presents Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), enhancing autoregressive robot policies by enabling tokens to iteratively refine action reconstructions, improving performance across various tasks.
机器人与自动化研究中心.debug_abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Jingjing Wei, Hao Zhao, Xinke Li, Linxi Yu, Xiaosong Gao
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: The MathVis benchmark evaluates LLMs' diagram-assisted reasoning in math problem visualization, revealing limitations in their ability to produce clear, visually coherent outputs.
机器人与自动化研究中心.debug_abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.

机器人与自动化研究中心.title: Watch, Recall, Act: Always-On Robots in Concurrent Embodied Streams
机器人与自动化研究中心.authors_text: Ding Yi, Peiwen Sun, Chenchu Rong, Jianan Wang, Xili Dai
机器人与自动化研究中心.summary: The paper introduces ARMS, an always-on robot capable of concurrent actions by integrating live perception and self-history, achieving superior performance in complex, dynamic environments.
机器人与自动化研究中心.debug_abstract: An always-on robot faces an endless stream that never resets: instructions arrive and lapse, the scene changes, and its own past actions reshape what it must reason about. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot policy research.

深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).authors_text: Dijia Zhan, Zhuo Li, Xuemiao Xu, Sun Zheng, Jinyi Li
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).summary: The paper presents Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), enhancing autoregressive robot policies by enabling tokens to iteratively refine action reconstructions, improving performance across various tasks.
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).debug_abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.

深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).title: Watch, Recall, Act: Always-On Robots in Concurrent Embodied Streams
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).authors_text: Ding Yi, Peiwen Sun, Chenchu Rong, Jianan Wang, Xili Dai
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).summary: The paper introduces ARMS, an always-on robot capable of concurrent actions by integrating live perception and self-history, achieving superior performance in complex, dynamic environments.
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).debug_abstract: An always-on robot faces an endless stream that never resets: instructions arrive and lapse, the scene changes, and its own past actions reshape what it must reason about. Today's action models are built for the opposite: a fixed instruction, no mid-task intervention, single-step reasoning. In an open-ended world a robot must watch a live stream for far-future cues, recall its own far-past actions, and act on them under dual-arm concurrency. We present ARMS (Always-on Robot in Multi-modal Streams), a deliberately simple streaming policy: a single pretrained $π$0.5 backbone augmented by three lightweight modules that turn live perception, embodied states, and the robot's own past actions into context the backbone reads before it acts. The modules update this context asynchronously, so watching and recalling never block acting and the two arms act at once. Rather than inventing new mechanisms, ARMS integrates these learned context providers with an agent-causal self-history that logs which arm did what, and when. To supervise them without extra annotation, we build ARMS Dataset, whose staged construction script itself labels every module from real dual-arm teleoperation. Trained on it, ARMS reaches 45% on the combined task against 28% for the strongest of our four main baselines, and ablations confirm the memory module, the embodied-state head, and asynchronous concurrency are each necessary.

深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).title: TaskAnchor: Grounding Task State in Reactive VLAs for Long-Horizon Manipulation
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).authors_text: Hengyan Liu, Wenlve Zhou, Bo Yue, Yongyi Su, Ruixiang Wang
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).summary: TaskAnchor enhances long-horizon manipulation in reactive VLAs by grounding task state through contextual input adaptation, significantly improving success rates without altering the backbone architecture.
深圳市人工智能与机器人研究院 (AIRS).debug_abstract: Reactive vision-language-action (VLA) policies suffer from task-state aliasing in long-horizon manipulation, where identical multimodal inputs call for distinct, context-dependent actions. Given that pretrained VLAs already possess rich control primitives to express diverse behaviors, we hypothesize that the execution bottleneck lies not in policy capacity, but in input ambiguity. In this paper, we propose TaskAnchor, a lightweight adapter that grounds task state by injecting execution context into the VLA's native input space. During post-training, TaskAnchor learns to represent the semantic execution stage as a milestone-supervised coordinate prepended to the language instruction, while incorporating fine-grained historical evidence via a residual update to the current visual tokens. This formulation avoids generating complex subtask instructions and leaves the backbone architecture unchanged. Across long-horizon benchmarks, TaskAnchor delivers substantial gains, achieving approximately 6 times the average success rate of the pi0.5 and X-VLA baselines on RMBench and more than doubling the task success rate of pi0.5 on RoboMemArena. Real-robot experiments further validate reliable multi-stage execution, with the same policy adapting its subsequent behaviors using earlier human interactions as in-context cues. Our project website is available at https://taskanchor.netlify.app/.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: PartiGen: Part-Aware Representations for Language-Conditioned Humanoid Motion Generation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Chuxuan Huang, Zhanxiang Cao, Tianyue Zhan, Haoyang Li, Yang Zhang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: PartiGen is a part-aware framework that generates humanoid motion from language by integrating anatomical structure and improving kinematic consistency, achieving significant performance enhancements in simulation and real execution.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Translating language into humanoid motion requires coordinating body parts, determining motion duration, and producing references suitable for robot execution. We introduce PartiGen, a part-aware latent diffusion framework that incorporates anatomical structure into a shared whole-body motion representation. Part-specific attention processes anatomically masked frame features, and its outputs are fused to combine local limb information with whole-body context. Conditioned on text and motion history, the model generates motion primitives autoregressively. Forward-kinematics supervision encourages kinematic consistency, while a learned end-of-sequence predictor selects a frame-level endpoint after generation. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, PartiGen achieves a segment-level FID of 3.165, a 16.8% reduction over TextOp, and improves R@1 by 1.4 percentage points. In the duration study with 16-frame primitives, endpoint prediction reduces mean absolute duration error from 12.471 to 3.080 frames compared with a fixed-length cutoff. We further evaluate robot execution using a pretrained, frozen GRIT tracker: 409 of 500 generated references (81.8%) pass the posture-based stability screen in MuJoCo. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 attempted motions are judged successful on the real G1.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jie Huang, Yanan Chen, Ruixun Liu, Kaichen He, Xinyi He
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: EmbodiedCLBench is a novel benchmark for assessing continual learning in self-evolving agents within embodied environments, revealing limitations and insights into skill transfer and task complexity.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: MIRAGE: Metric Inference and Reliability-Aware Gaussian Estimation from Feed-Forward Vision
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xinzhe Wang, Changjian Jiang, Kaiwen Song, Xudong Li, Kerui Ren
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: MIRAGE integrates feed-forward visual geometry with LiDAR-IMU data for accurate metric pose estimation and high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction, outperforming existing vision-only methods.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Feed-forward 3D priors enable high-quality reconstruction from image streams but often lack reliable metric scale and suffer from long-term trajectory drift. In contrast, LiDAR--inertial estimation provides metrically accurate motion but lacks the image-space consistency needed for high-fidelity reconstruction. We propose $MIRAGE$, which anchors feed-forward visual geometry to LiDAR--IMU metric motion and regulates online pose corrections according to correspondence support and cross-modal agreement, jointly enabling accurate metric pose estimation and high-fidelity Gaussian reconstruction. Experiments on Oxford Spires, M2DGR and INS show that MIRAGE achieves accurate metric trajectory estimation, outperforming COLMAP, a widely used but computationally expensive reference for vision-only benchmarks. Motivated by the scarcity of long-horizon monocular benchmarks for large-scale indoor reconstruction, we further build a multimodal data-collection platform and use MIRAGE to establish accurate 6-DoF reference trajectories for a new vision-only benchmark. We benchmark recent monocular large-scale reconstruction methods on this dataset, providing a systematic evaluation of their performance in long-horizon indoor scenes.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: MagCilia: A Compact Magnetociliary Tactile Sensor with 3D Force Sensing for Robotic Contact Perception and Grasping Feedback
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yu Feng, Hao Wu, Haotian Guo, Haoming Liu, William Su
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The MagCilia sensor integrates flexible magnetic-cilia structures and Hall sensors for precise 3D force sensing, enhancing robotic grasping and surface recognition capabilities.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Robotic grasping and surface exploration benefit from simultaneous measurement of normal and tangential forces and from surface information obtained through contact. Here, we present a compact magnetociliary tactile sensor (MagCilia) that combines a flexible magnetic-cilia structure with a Hall sensor for 3D force sensing. Quasi-static finite element analysis is used to investigate structural deformation and magnetic responses under multidirectional loading. To reconstruct forces from the coupled magnetic channels, we propose causal history fusion regression (CHFR), which combines current magnetic-field measurements with their recent changes. Five-fold cross-validation grouped by calibration record yields root-mean-square errors of 0.40, 0.57, and 0.69 N for Fx, Fy, and Fz, respectively, with corresponding coefficients of determination of 0.93, 0.90, and 0.92. Robotic experiments demonstrate tangential-force-guided gripper adjustment and multi-axis load monitoring under external perturbations. Frequency-domain features of the reconstructed forces distinguish six surface categories with 99.39% accuracy in three-fold cross-validation grouped by acquisition session. An online robotic demonstration additionally identifies all six tested surfaces. These results demonstrate 3D force reconstruction, grasping feedback, and surface recognition using a single compact tactile unit.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Spatial Memory Intelligence: Endowing World Models with Understanding-Driven Long-Term Memory
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ying Yang, Guiyu Zhang, Lianghua Huang, Chang Nie, Chenyang Si
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper introduces Spatial Memory Intelligence (SMI), a framework enhancing long-video world models with systematic spatial-memory management through four coordinated operations, improving memory efficiency and generation quality.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Long-video generation and world models have shown strong potential for interactive entertainment and embodied simulation by predicting future observations conditioned on user actions and historical memory. However, as memory sequences grow longer and their structures become increasingly complex, managing long-range spatial context becomes increasingly challenging, calling for a more intelligent and systematic memory-management strategy. Building on the advancing spatial reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and the broader vision of unified models, we propose Spatial Memory Intelligence (SMI), the first framework to systematically employ an understanding model for spatial-memory management in long-video world models. SMI introduces four coordinated atomic operations: spatial clustering, within-cluster sparsification, action-aware retrieval, and reliability-aware filtering. Extensive experiments across multiple baselines, benchmarks, and world-model backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of SMI, achieving comprehensive improvements in memory sparsity, generation stability, and spatial consistency.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Object Concepts Emerge from Motion
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Boshi Li, Xiaohui Wang, Xiaoyang Wu, Zhichao Li, Ya Yang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper introduces a motion-based framework for learning object-centric visual representations from videos, achieving superior performance in various tasks without requiring human annotations.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Object-centric visual representations are important for physical-world perception, but existing visual pretraining methods often capture semantic categories without preserving the identity and coherence of individual instances. We present a biologically inspired framework that learns object-centric representations for single images from raw videos. Our approach uses motion boundaries as a source of object-level grouping: off-the-shelf optical flow and clustering produce pseudo-instance masks, which supervise a single-image encoder with pixel-level pairwise metric learning. The framework requires neither human annotations nor camera calibration. We first obtain 195 million pseudo-labeled frames from 7,163 hours of driving and web videos, then expand the supervision to 421 million frames with Motion-Verified Self-Training, which combines model proposals with motion evidence. We train encoders up to Swin-H and distill the learned representations into a family of Swin backbones. Across monocular depth estimation, 3D object detection, 3D occupancy prediction, and end-to-end planning, the resulting models achieve competitive or superior performance relative to supervised and self-supervised pretraining baselines, with particularly strong transfer on geometry- and instance-sensitive tasks. These results show that motion-derived supervision can teach static image encoders to represent visual instances, providing a complementary direction for scalable visual pretraining.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Latent Reward Steering: An Adaptive Inference-Time Framework that Implicitly Promotes Cognitive Behaviors in Reasoning LLMs
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jiakang Li, Guanyu Zhu, Can Jin, Chenxi Huang, Dexu Yu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Latent Reward Steering (LRS) enhances reasoning in LLMs by adaptively optimizing latent states based on reward signals, improving cognitive behavior deployment during inference.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Strong reasoning depends not only on model knowledge but also on how effectively cognitive behaviors are deployed during generation. Existing methods often rely on explicit behavior-level control, making them insufficiently adaptive when failures and required corrections vary across reasoning states, tasks, and models. To this end, we propose Latent Reward Steering (LRS), an adaptive inference-time framework that promotes cognitive behaviors by optimizing the sparse-autoencoder (SAE) latent states that implicitly carry them. Rather than relying on predefined cognitive behaviors or steering directions derived from them, LRS trains a latent reward model on reasoning traces by final answer correctness to estimate the quality of intermediate latent states. During inference, reward gradients provide state-specific correction directions for fragile latent states, while a reward and confidence gate restricts intervention to states the reward signal flags as fragile. Experiments on multiple reasoning LLM backbones and benchmarks show that \ours consistently improves performance over various baselines, and post-hoc analyses further indicate that \ours implicitly promotes good cognitive behaviors that fix the original reasoning errors. Code is available at: https://github.com/jiakanglee/Latent-Reward-Steering.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: SAP-CoPE: Social-Aware Planning using Cooperative Pose Estimation with Infrastructure Sensor Nodes
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Minghao Ning, Yufeng Yang, Shucheng Huang, Jiaming Zhong, Keqi Shu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: SAP-CoPE is an indoor navigation framework that combines cooperative sensing, human pose estimation, and social-aware motion planning to enhance robot interactions in human-populated environments.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Autonomous mobile robots must operate smoothly in human-populated indoor environments, where onboard-only sensing suffers from limited perception range and occlusions, and socially compliant motion planning must account for human psychological comfort zones. These factors complicate accurate recognition of human intentions and the generation of comfortable, social-aware trajectories. To address these challenges, we propose SAP-CoPE, an indoor navigation framework that integrates cooperative infrastructure sensing, human pose estimation, and a social-aware MPC planner. In the perception module, an uncertainty-aware optimization problem is formulated to estimate 3D human poses from camera observations, with optional incorporation of sparse LiDAR point-cloud measurements, while considering human joint coherence. In the planning module, the estimated human pose and orientation are used to construct a personal-space (PS) field within an MPC framework, enabling the robot to account for both physical safety and psychological comfort. Extensive real-world evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in generating social-aware trajectories for autonomous systems.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yuhong Liu, Shenxi Wu, Junyi Chi, Beichen Zhang, Xuanlang Dai
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: SpatialASM enhances Large Vision-Language Models by integrating Active Spatial Mentalization through training-time spatial simulation, improving their spatial reasoning capabilities across multiple benchmarks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: MC-EvoBench is a controlled Minecraft benchmark designed to evaluate and audit the transferability and durability of embodied capabilities in self-improving agents.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: SimVTA: Simulation-Grounded Video-Trajectory Alignment for Driving World Action Models
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Changhui Jing, Haochen Tian, Hongchen Li, Tianyu Li, Caojun Wang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: SimVTA enhances driving world action models by integrating simulation-grounded video supervision for trajectory optimization, significantly improving planning performance in real-world scenarios.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Driving world action models (WAMs) learn from paired trajectories and future observations. Post-training with reinforcement learning allows the policy to explore alternative trajectories and improve planning using driving rewards. However, driving logs contain future videos only for the recorded trajectories, leaving these alternatives without corresponding visual supervision. Thus, we introduce SimVTA, a simulation-grounded post-training framework that combines trajectory optimization with video supervision. First, we sample candidate trajectories for each observation and use a real-world simulator (e.g., World Engine) to render future videos for high-reward candidates in real-world scenes reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). This provides trajectory-matched supervision independent of the model's own predictions. Under a limited rendering budget, we prioritize video supervision for higher-error futures among these rendered candidates. Finally, we optimize trajectory planning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and use a flow-matching loss on the matched videos to update shared representations. At inference time, the model predicts trajectories directly, without simulator calls. On NAVSIM v1, applying SimVTA to a WAM initialization improves PDMS from 86.2 to 91.3 (+5.1). It achieves 88.2 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and an average HD-Score of 38.8 in closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM. Ablations show that updating shared representations with video supervision improves planning, while prioritizing higher-error futures among high-reward trajectories further improves performance.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Chi Kit Ng, Yidong Zhang, Tianchun Wu, Siu Hing Lui, Hanlin Zhao
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: EndoRSI is a self-improving robotic system that refines endoscopic policies through iterative physical experimentation and human oversight, significantly enhancing insertion success rates.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jingjing Wei, Hao Zhao, Xinke Li, Linxi Yu, Xiaosong Gao
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The MathVis benchmark evaluates LLMs' diagram-assisted reasoning in math problem visualization, revealing limitations in their ability to produce clear, visually coherent outputs.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: KineWorld: Action-Induced Transport Fields for Embodied World Modeling
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ziying Song, Yuchen Liu, Zhuoran Xu, Ziyang Liu, Jian Jin
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: KineWorld introduces a transport-aware framework for embodied world modeling, enhancing action prediction by aligning visual generation with critical spatial changes in robot interactions.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Embodied world models predict the visual consequences of candidate actions before execution. However, existing action-conditioned world models often adopt uniformly weighted visual generation objectives that can be misaligned with embodied prediction needs. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs renderer-derived, camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates their motion support on the video-latent grid and reweights future-RGB flow matching through a normalized mixture of uniform and transport-focused distributions. We train KineWorld using ALOHA-AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0. KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 in single-view evaluation and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in multi-view evaluation. These results support a shift from appearance fitting toward action-consequence modeling for embodied decision-making.
